summary: How digital circuits work: binary, logic gates, TTL chips, flip-flops and multivibrators, memory, microprocessors, converters and counters.

blocks.title: Bits and levels
items: Analog takes any voltage. Digital has 2 levels, high and low, for 1 and 0. Each 1 or 0 is a bit.
Positive logic: high = 1, low = 0. Negative logic: high = 0, low = 1.
Binary places are 8, 4, 2, 1, so the quantity 2 is 0010.
BCD, binary coded decimal: each decimal digit gets its own 4 bits, so 25 is 0010 0101.

blocks.title: TTL chips
items: TTL, transistor-transistor logic: bipolar transistors do the gating and the output amplification.
Open input: no current flows out of it, so it acts high.
Check TTL with a logic probe: high, low or pulsing. A VOM or DMM shows only an average.

blocks.title: Flip-flops
items: A flip-flop is a binary sequential logic element with 2 stable states. It stores 1 bit.
A register is a row of them: 8 bits need 8 R-S flip-flops.
Clocked R-S: S and R wait for CLK, the clock (synchronous). PRE, preset, forces 1 and CLR, clear, forces 0 without it (asynchronous), overriding R and S.
A toggling flip-flop (J-K or T) halves the frequency. R-S can't toggle with R-S inputs held constant.

blocks.title: Exam traps
items: A transition isn't a level, so "transition level" choices are wrong.
NOR gives 1 only when all inputs are 0.
Both inputs high: AND goes high; NAND, NOR and XOR go low.
